questions.q: What are the three core EDR response actions covered in this lesson?
options: Isolate the host, kill the malicious process, and quarantine the file
Reboot the host, reinstall the operating system, and change all passwords
Send an email alert, log the event, and wait for the next scheduled scan
Format the hard drive, replace the hardware, and reimage the machine
questions.explain: These three actions -- isolate, kill process, and quarantine file -- cover the overwhelming majority of real EDR responses to a confirmed compromise.

questions.q: What does host isolation actually do to a compromised machine?
options: Cuts off nearly all normal network traffic while leaving the machine running and reachable through a secure channel to the EDR console
Immediately powers the machine off to stop all activity
Deletes every file on the machine automatically
Disconnects the machine from electrical power only, leaving the network connection active
questions.explain: Isolation cuts off the host's normal network paths while keeping it running and reachable through a dedicated secure channel to the EDR agent/console.

questions.q: Why is isolating a host usually preferred over powering it off?
options: Powering off destroys volatile memory (RAM) evidence -- running processes, injected code, connection state -- that a fileless or memory-resident attack never wrote to disk in the first place
Powering off takes longer than isolating a host
Isolated hosts automatically repair themselves
Powering off is not technically possible on most endpoints
questions.explain: A fileless attack's evidence often lives only in RAM; isolating the host keeps it running so that evidence survives for investigation, while a power-off erases it.

questions.q: What is the difference between killing a process and quarantining a file?
options: Killing a process stops a specific running malicious process immediately without taking the host offline; quarantining a file moves or encrypts a malicious file so it can no longer execute
They are two names for exactly the same action
Killing a process only works on Linux; quarantining a file only works on Windows
Quarantining a file requires the host to be powered off first
questions.explain: Killing a process targets a running process directly, while quarantining a file acts on a file so it can't be executed again -- both are narrower, faster tools than full isolation.

questions.q: In the containment example, why didn't the analyst simply power off all four machines?
options: Doing so would have destroyed the memory-resident evidence showing exactly how the attacker moved between machines; isolating instead kept them running for investigation while still stopping further spread
Powering off machines is against company policy in all cases
The machines could not be powered off remotely
Powering off would have alerted the attacker immediately
questions.explain: Isolating the compromised host and using kill/quarantine on the others stopped the activity while preserving the live evidence a shutdown would have erased.
